```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3, fig.align = "center")
library(ggplot2)
```

## Overview

I simulate the exponential distribution (rate $\lambda = 0.2$) and study the mean of 40
draws, repeated 1000 times. By the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) these averages should be
approximately normal, centred at $1/\lambda = 5$ with standard deviation
$(1/\lambda)/\sqrt{40} \approx 0.79$. I compare the simulated mean, variance and shape with theory.
Code is in the appendix.

## Simulations

`rexp(40, 0.2)` gives 40 exponentials; I take their mean and repeat this 1000 times
(seed fixed for reproducibility). For contrast I also draw 1000 individual exponentials.

```{r sim, echo=TRUE}
set.seed(123)
lambda <- 0.2; n <- 40; nsim <- 1000
means  <- replicate(nsim, mean(rexp(n, lambda)))
single <- rexp(nsim, lambda)
```

## Sample mean versus theoretical mean

```{r mean}
th_mean <- 1 / lambda
sm <- mean(means)
```

The theoretical mean is $1/\lambda =$ `r th_mean`; the mean of the 1000 averages is
**`r round(sm, 3)`**, a difference of `r round(abs(sm - th_mean), 3)`. The sample mean of averages is an
unbiased estimate of the population mean, so the two agree closely (Figure 1, red = sample mean, blue = theory, almost overlapping).

## Sample variance versus theoretical variance

```{r var}
th_var <- (1 / lambda)^2 / n
sv <- var(means)
```

The variance of a mean of $n$ draws is $\sigma^2/n = (1/\lambda)^2/40 =$ **`r round(th_var, 3)`**
(sd `r round(sqrt(th_var), 3)`). The simulated variance is **`r round(sv, 3)`** (sd `r round(sd(means), 3)`).
They agree to within simulation noise. By contrast, a single exponential has variance 25, so
averaging 40 values cuts the variance by a factor of 40.

## Distribution

```{r hist, fig.cap="Figure 1: 1000 averages of 40 exponentials, with the sample mean (red), theoretical mean (blue) and the normal density predicted by the CLT (dark curve)."}
ggplot(data.frame(m = means), aes(m)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = th_mean, sd = sqrt(th_var)), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = th_mean, colour = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sm, colour = "red", linetype = 2, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean of 40 exponentials", y = "Density") + theme_minimal()
```

```{r cmp, fig.height=2.8, fig.cap="Figure 2: 1000 individual exponentials (left) are strongly right-skewed; 1000 averages of 40 (right) are bell-shaped. See Figure 3 for the Q-Q plot."}
d <- rbind(data.frame(x = single, type = "Individual exponentials"),
           data.frame(x = means,  type = "Averages of 40"))
ggplot(d, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") + theme_minimal()
```

The individual exponentials follow the skewed exponential shape (a spike near 0 and a long tail),
whereas the averages are symmetric and match the overlaid normal curve. The Q-Q plot confirms
this: points lie close to the line except for slight deviation in the extreme tails, where
the residual right-skew of the exponential is still faintly visible at $n=40$.

```{r qq, fig.height=2.8, fig.cap="Figure 3: Normal Q-Q plot of the 1000 averages."}
qqnorm(means, main = ""); qqline(means, col = "red")
```

As a coverage check, `r round(mean(abs(means - th_mean) < 1.96*sqrt(th_var))*100, 1)`% of averages fall within
$\pm 1.96$ theoretical sd of 5 (normal theory: 95%).

## Appendix: code

```{r appendix, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(123); lambda <- 0.2; n <- 40; nsim <- 1000
means  <- replicate(nsim, mean(rexp(n, lambda)))
single <- rexp(nsim, lambda)
mean(means); 1/lambda                 # sample vs theoretical mean
var(means);  (1/lambda)^2 / n         # sample vs theoretical variance
hist(means, freq = FALSE); curve(dnorm(x, 5, sqrt(25/40)), add = TRUE)
qqnorm(means); qqline(means)
```
